job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room in a flat in Valencia with my cousin Marcos, and my days run on a loop. In the morning I check job boards and send maybe five applications, then I spend a couple of hours on a small project, a solar panel monitor I'm building from a spare board. Afternoons I run or play five-a-side with friends from the university. I finished electrical engineering six months ago and still have no offer.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a bit about the final project and the internships.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was a fault detector for solar inverters, and it got the top mark. I did one internship at the regional grid operator and one at a wind turbine maintenance company, where I climbed a tower once and nearly lost my breakfast. I liked the mix of screens and real equipment. My references are strong, so the silence is confusing, but I know hiring in engineering moves slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine, we've heard this movie before. Tools get a bit better, some paperwork shrinks, and the world still needs people to fix a transformer at three in the morning. I'd tell friends to stay calm and keep applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit relieved, because my field is half screen and half physical, and that suits a slow plateau. What bothers me is that the plateau hasn't helped me get an offer yet. Six months without one is long, even with strong references.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aim for grid operators and energy firms rather than software shops, and ask my old supervisor at the grid operator for a recommendation call. I'd also finish the solar monitor and put it on a simple website. I wouldn't change my savings plan, since my parents and my own money give me about eight months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm, honestly. I'd be impatient but not worried about the long run. A plateau is a world where my training keeps its worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a friend who is more worried than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would make you more sure about your first job?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has the grid operator's work taught you about how fast things really change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A real person who says yes. An offer letter would fix most of this. I'd say the weak point is that everyone wants two years of experience for a first role, which is a bit of a joke. The grid is old and short of engineers, so I think my turn will come.

say: I'd tell friends we've heard this before and the world still needs people to fix **transformers** at night.
I'd say stay calm and **keep applying**.
think: My field is half screen, half **equipment**, so a slow plateau suits me.
Six months without an **offer** bothers me more than any AI news.
do: Aim for **grid operators** and energy firms, not software shops.
Ask my old supervisor for a **recommendation** call.
Finish the solar monitor and put it on a simple **website**.
feel: Quite **calm**, impatient but not worried about the long run.
S0.quote: The world still needs people to fix a transformer at three in the morning.
fieldNote: He sees the physical half of his field as **protection**.
The real irritant is the six-month **wait**, not AI.
Strong savings and many openings nearby keep him calm.

steps.text: Send five applications a day to Valencia energy and grid firms
Ask the grid operator supervisor to call two hiring managers
Finish the solar monitor and offer it to local small businesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real but manageable, and unions and regulators should keep an eye on how it's rolled out. In my field the drawing checks, report writing and spreadsheet work could be done by software. I'd tell friends to learn the tools and not just complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel a pinch, because the junior jobs in engineering are exactly the report and checking work. The entry-level posts at big firms might shrink first. But anyone who can inspect a real substation and also use the software will be wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using an AI tool for my simulation reports and code, and learn it properly, not just once in a while. I'd look for hybrid roles in maintenance and commissioning where a person must be on site. I'd also join the young engineers' branch of the union at the grid operator, because they're pushing for training rights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little tense but not frightened. It's like when the internship moved from paper logs to a tablet: annoying for a week, then normal. My cushion lets me adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of an engineer's early work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which tasks do you do now with AI, and which would you never hand over?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the people in your five-a-side group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it now and then for explaining code errors. I'd never hand over the safety sign-off, though. If a protection relay is set wrong, people get hurt, and I want a named human to answer for it. That is also where I see my own future.

say: I'd say it's real but **manageable**, and regulators should watch the roll-out.
I'd tell friends to **learn** the tools instead of complaining.
think: Junior **report** and checking work could shrink first, and that's where I'd start.
People who can inspect real **equipment** and use software will still be wanted.
do: Learn an **AI tool** properly for my simulation reports and code.
Look for **commissioning** and maintenance roles where a person must be on site.
Join the young engineers' branch of the **union**.
feel: A little **tense**, but it's like the move from paper logs to a tablet.
S1.quote: I'd never hand over the safety sign-off, though. If a protection relay is set wrong, people get hurt, and I want a named human to answer for it.
fieldNote: He picks **site-based** work as the safe zone and says so concretely.
Willing to adopt tools, but draws a firm line at **safety** sign-off.
Union leanings show up as practical, not angry.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant for simulation reports for a month
Apply to commissioning and maintenance roles at substations
Join the young engineers' union branch at the grid operator

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need an emergency plan: income support, retraining, rules that slow down firms. I'd march if there was a march, and I'd say it online too. This can't be left to markets alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it's frightening, because the thinking half of my job goes first, and I'd lose the design and analysis work that makes engineering interesting. The hands-on half survives until about 2031, but not forever. Two years isn't enough to build a safe position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any hands-on job in energy, even a technician post, quickly, because physical work gets me three extra years. I'd learn electrician-level skills, like wiring and testing, in evening classes. I'd cut my spending to the basics and keep my savings for a rainy period, and I'd move back to my parents' house to save on rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing in front of a big wave, but I'm not frozen. I'm anxious, mostly for the people who have no savings. I'd keep telling myself that I still have hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years, robots by 2031. Which of your skills last the longest, and by how much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Design and analysis go first. My hands-on skills, like wiring and testing in a substation, last until around 2031, which is a real three years. After that, I don't know, and I'd say that honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in your flat with Marcos when you hear this news?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcos would panic and want to leave the city. I'd say let's stay calm, share rent, and look at the jobs on the coast and on the wind farms together. I like being the one who reads the room, but I'd be shaken too.

say: I'd say governments need an **emergency plan** with income support and retraining.
I'd go to a **march** if there was one, and post online too.
think: The **thinking** half of my job goes first, including design and analysis.
Hands-on work buys me about **three years**, not forever.
do: Take any hands-on **technician** job in energy, quickly.
Learn **wiring** and testing skills in evening classes.
Cut spending to basics and move back to my **parents'** house.
feel: Like standing in front of a **big wave**, but not frozen.
S2.quote: My hands-on skills, like wiring and testing in a substation, last until around 2031, which is a real three years.
fieldNote: He splits his field in two: the **thinking** half goes first, the hands-on half later.
Moves to a **technician** route rather than waiting for design jobs.
Has a clear plan and savings, so stays anxious, not alarmed.

steps.text: Apply for substation technician roles on the Valencia coast
Take evening classes in industrial wiring and testing
Cut spending to rent, food and transport only
Move back to my parents' house to save rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if governments and unions get moving. I'd push for retraining funds paid by AI companies. And I'd say to my friends: don't wait for permission to train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel uneasy but not frightened. I could get a first job, build three years of real site experience, and be among the people who know both the equipment and the software. That makes me useful for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a first job in energy, then do a part-time master's in power systems with company support. I'd learn the AI tools seriously, so I'm the one who supervises them. I'd also keep saving, because even a good plan needs a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit better than the two-year picture. It's like being told that a storm is coming in five days. You still board the windows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rules, yes, because without them the gains would go to a few firms. A new tax or a levy on big automation could fund training. I wouldn't say it's too late, but it would need to start soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still push for rules, or is it too late?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra three years let me build real credibility. At the grid operator a senior told me something I won't forget. People with years on site are trusted more than clever beginners, and I want to become one of those trusted engineers before the robots catch up.

I'd push for retraining funds paid by **AI companies**.
think: I'd feel **uneasy** but not frightened, with time to build site experience.
Knowing both **equipment** and software would make me useful for a while.

S3.quote: People with years on site are trusted more than clever beginners, and I want to become one of those trusted engineers before the robots catch up.
fieldNote: Extra time turns **dread** into a career ladder.

steps.text: Accept a first engineer role at an energy firm near Valencia
Start a part-time master's in power systems
Practise supervising AI design tools on real grid cases
Save 30 percent of every pay cheque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a chance to get it right, and I'd call for a proper plan: shorter working weeks, public funds, and new rights to training. I'd be fairly relaxed in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm. By 33 I'd have a full career, maybe senior on a wind farm. The change would still come, but I'd have time to move into work that needs people, like field service and safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, save, and buy a small flat with Marcos' sister, who is an architect, if rates allow. I'd become a good field engineer, learn the tools one by one, and keep improving my skills. I'd also take a role in the union branch so I speak for younger staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels fine, honestly, like planning for retirement. Not exciting, but not frightening either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if people push. In my region the wind and solar boom has already moved a lot of money around, and I've seen decent plans for training. With ten years, I'd trust that something works out, but it needs pressure from workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think society handles this well, given that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the same things, just calmer. Ten years makes room for learning Portuguese, since the energy market there is growing. That feels nice.

say: I'd say ten years lets us get it right with **public funds** and training rights.
think: I'm **calm**: by 33 I'd be a senior field engineer.
Ten years lets me move into work that needs **people**, like field service and safety.

Become a strong **field engineer** and learn the tools one by one.
Take a role in the **union** branch for younger staff.

His **union** instinct stays in the background.

steps.text: Work as a field engineer on wind and solar sites
Save a deposit for a small flat in Valencia

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. The robots arrive three years later, but the design work disappears right away, and I'd have no time to build experience. What would help is training paid by the firms that profit, plus real support for the first job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I am lucky, and I know it. Plenty of my classmates can't wait six months without an offer. Strong savings and a supportive family mean I can, and I'd like the study to remember them.

headlineQuote: I am lucky, and I know it. Plenty of my classmates can't wait six months without an offer.
portrait: Pedro is **23**, an electrical engineer from Valencia with top grades, sharing a rented room with his cousin.
He splits his field into a thinking half that AI takes first and a **hands-on** half that lasts longer.
He uses AI tools now and then and will learn them properly if needed, with a firm line at **safety** sign-off.
He leans left, wants unions and public **training** funds, and stays calmer than most thanks to savings.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, because design work would vanish before he builds site experience.
whatWouldHelp: Retraining paid by profiting firms and real support for a **first job**.
